tier_reason: benchmarks/README.md links per-size CSVs for Sleipnir and CasADi+Ipopt+MUMPS, generated by benchmarks/generate-scalability-results.sh from public sources in benchmarks/scalability/{flywheel,cart_pole}; it states g++ (GCC) 16.2.1 and an AMD Ryzen 7 7840U, and its build command sets no build type, so the root CMakeLists.txt default RelWithDebInfo (CMake GCC default -O2 -g -DNDEBUG) plus -Wall -Wextra -pedantic and C++23 from cmake/CompilerFlags.cmake fixes the flags. This follows the wave-1 precedent that a CMake default build type counts as stated flags.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810. The README build command (cmake -B build -S . -DSLEIPNIR_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON) sets no build type, so the root CMakeLists.txt default RelWithDebInfo applies (CMake's GCC default -O2 -g -DNDEBUG), with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic and C++23 from cmake/CompilerFlags.cmake; no -march. The build flags of the CasADi, Ipopt and MUMPS binaries are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Compares a full AD plus interior-point stack against CasADi plus Ipopt plus MUMPS, so AD speed alone is not isolated. CasADi uses tuned options (expand=true, constant Hessian/Jacobian hints on flywheel) while Sleipnir uses defaults. Sleipnir's cart-pole solve times are slower than CasADi from 150 samples up (for example 3065.18 ms vs 973.846 ms at 250 samples; the Sleipnir cart-pole CSV has no 200-sample row), possibly because of different iteration counts. Flags come from the CMake default build type rather than a listed flag string, and the README's run step names ./tools/generate-scalability-results.sh while the script actually lives at benchmarks/generate-scalability-results.sh. Author's own benchmark; the README notes commercial linear solvers could make Ipopt much faster.

notes: All eight claimed numbers match the CSVs exactly (flywheel 1000 and 5000 samples, cart-pole 300 samples). Metadata checked on github.com: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt), 80 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-09-27. Fits autodiff-and-ml-kernels as an AD library, though the measured workload is a full NLP solve (sparse-and-solvers would also fit).

tier_reason: First-party README tables of average percent gains over torch.matmul, cuBLAS and cuBLASLt, backed by public per-shape CSVs in eval_results/ and the harness (eval_one_file.sh, benchmarking_offline.py, benchmarking_server.py, tools/utils.py, which sets the nvcc flags). The CUDA toolkit/nvcc version is not stated in the repo, and the arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed as far as seen) could not be opened, so A and B are both out of reach.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: nvcc through torch.utils.cpp_extension.load with -O3 -std=c++17 --use_fast_math --expt-relaxed-constexpr --expt-extended-lambda (tools/utils.py get_build_cuda_cflags); TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST 8.0 for A100/RTX 3090 and 9.0a for H100; CUTLASS v4.2.1 and PyTorch >= 2.6.0. The CUDA toolkit/nvcc version is not stated.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README, average gains over 1,000 (M,N,K) shapes, vs torch.matmul / cuBLAS / cuBLASLt-heuristic / cuBLASLt-AutoTuning. A100 F32F16F16F32: offline +22.5% / +20.4% / +16.9% / +12.2%, server +25.1% / +21.5% / +19.9% / +12.7%. H100 F32F16F16F32: offline +19.8% / +17.5% / +28.8% / +7.0%, server +41.7% / +40.5% / +42.1% / +22.1%. RTX 3090 F32F16F16F32: offline +21.3% / +24.2% / +21.1% / +12.7%, server +28.7% / +35.3% / +28.1% / +19.8%. A100 F16F16F16F16: offline +22.0% / +19.2% / +16.8% / +11.4%, server +28.7% / +26.0% / +22.4% / +15.9%. From the per-shape offline CSVs (derived from page data): the README figures are arithmetic means of per-shape speedups; the geometric mean vs cuBLASLt-AutoTuning is 1.11x on A100 and 1.056x on H100.
corrections.caveats: Plain HGEMM against cuBLAS, so it belongs closer to blas-lapack than to DL-layer kernels; baseline_in_list is false because cuDNN, oneDNN, XNNPACK and Eigen are not the comparison. Gains are per-shape averages for the 1,000 released shapes only (other shapes need zero-padding to the nearest released one), and the kernels are tuned per GPU. Per-shape offline CSVs in eval_results/ (derived from page data): CUDA-L2 is slower than cuBLASLt-AutoTuning on 300 of 1,000 shapes on A100 (worst 0.545x) and 338 of 1,000 on H100 (worst 0.209x); for the 64 shapes with M, N and K all >= 4096 the mean is 0.986x (A100) and 0.928x (H100), so the win concentrates on small and skinny shapes. The kernels build with --use_fast_math. The CUDA toolkit version is not stated, and the paper (arXiv 2512.02551) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked). The repo was first published as deepreinforce-ai/CUDA-L2 (LICENSE copyright deepreinforce.ai).

notes: README numbers match the record, and the A100 F32 offline means re-derive exactly from eval_results/cuda_l2_a100_F32F16F16F32_speedup_offline.csv (1.2248, 1.2042, 1.1694, 1.1216). Metadata from github.com: MIT, 482 stars, 32 forks, not a fork or archived, last commit 2026-03-30. Consider moving it to blas-lapack; it is slower than tuned cuBLASLt on large square GEMMs.

tier_reason: First-party: the repo description claims 3.3x over the ONNX Runtime graph and the README gives the runtime's own RTF tables (Apple M2, Galaxy S23+) and PESQ against fp32 ONNX, but the ONNX Runtime timing and its harness are not in the public repo, and the compiler is not named.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release with -O3 -Wall -Wextra (no -ffast-math) and per-file tier flags (-march=armv8.2-a+dotprod, -march=armv8.6-a+dotprod+i8mm; x86 -mavx2 -mfma, plus -mavxvnni or -mavx512f/bw/vl/vnni), with optional PGO; the compiler and its version are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The 3.3x figure is only in the repository description; the README tables time faster-enhancer.c alone and give no ONNX Runtime timing. A search-engine snippet of the arXiv abstract (2607.25350; arxiv.org could not be opened here) gives 0.069 RTF vs 0.230 for the fp32 ONNX Runtime graph on the same M2 core; the ORT version, thread count and execution provider were not seen. docs/optimizations.md says the ONNX benchmark logs and scripts are committed under experiments/, but the public repo has no experiments/ directory (404), so the baseline timing cannot be reproduced from the repo. The comparison is int8 W8A8 against an fp32 graph, so precision differs (PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060). The x86 tiers are not timed in the README, and the docs say the x86 rows of the paper's Table 1 have no artifact. A paced real-time callback costs 4.2x more per frame (0.286 RTF) than the racing benchmark. Single-model runtime, not a general kernel library.

notes: README numbers (0.069 / 0.096 RTF, PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060, 824 utterances, 4.2x paced cost) match the record. Metadata from github.com: MIT, 25 stars, 5 forks, not a fork or archived, 4 commits, last 2026-07-29. A docs claim of committed ONNX benchmark artifacts is not borne out by the public tree; worth recording as a reproducibility shortcoming.
